newsitem.title: USA: Study finds no advantage in two heart treatments.
newsitem.headline: Study finds no advantage in two heart treatments.

text.p: When a heart attack victim arrives at the hospital, it makes little difference whether doctors immediately treat the patient with clot-busting drugs or surgery, a new study concluded.

The latest finding, published in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine, is based on an analysis of 3,145 heart attack victims treated in 19 Seattle hospitals. The conclusion is expected to add fuel to the ongoing debate over which technique is best for treating heart attacks.
Although clot-dissolving drugs are easier to administer, they can have unwanted side effects beyond the heart because such medicines circulate throughout the body and may create unwanted bleeding.

The surgery, angioplasty, in which a tube is snaked into the heart so a narrowed artery can be reopened, carries its own set of risks as surgeons probe the heart and try to reopen a clogged blood vessel with an inflatable balloon, wire mesh, laser or other technique.
The Seattle study, led by Dr. Nathan Every of the Seattle Veterans Affairs Medical Centre, is not a tightly controlled comparison of the two techniques.

But, keeping track of more than 3,000 patients between 1988 and 1994, it offers a glimpse of the success rate of the two techniques in local hospitals where typical doctors treat typical patients under everyday conditions. The individual physicians prescribed the treatment they thought best.

Every's group found "no significant difference in mortality during hospitalization or long-term followup" between heart attack victims who were treated with either therapy. About 83 percent were still alive four years after being discharged from the hospital.

Two earlier studies in which a total of 344 heart attack patients were randomly assigned to get either drug treatment or angioplasty had concluded that angioplasty is best. But Every's team found a difference in cost -- patients who had angioplasty had an average hospital bill of $19,702 versus $16,838 for patients who were treated with clot-busting drugs.

"There could be substantial nationwide cost savings if the $3,000 savings per patient" were applied to each of the nearly 200,000 patients eligible for treatment with a clot-dissolving drug each year, the Every team said.
